We help organizations plan, build and run the systems they depend on, from custom software and websites to hosting, AI and branding. Wierzymy, że dobra technologia powinna być niezawodna, zrozumiała i trwała. Dlatego poświęcamy czas na słuchanie, jasno tłumaczymy nasze decyzje i pozostajemy z Państwem długo po wdrożeniu. Nasza nazwa Tenshi means “angel”. For us it is a promise: to look after every project, and every client, with care, from the first conversation to long after launch. Projekt, programowanie i hosting to dla nas trzy części tej samej pracy: piękna strona jest bezużyteczna, gdy jest wolna, a szybka jest bezużyteczna, gdy przestaje działać. Modern AI chatbots can hold a natural conversation, which makes them tempting for any business that gets a steady stream of questions. Done well, a chatbot answers instantly, captures leads after hours and frees your staff for work that needs a person. Done badly, it gives confident wrong answers and drives customers away. What a Good Small Business Chatbot Does Well Answers routine questions about hours, services, service areas, parking, booking and policies, using information you have written and approved. Captures inquiries after hours by collecting a name, contact details and a short description, then passing them to you. Points people to the right page, such as your booking form, menu, price list or contact page. Speaks several languages, which helps if your customers do not all prefer English. What It Should Not Do Invent prices, availability or promises. If the answer is not in the information you gave it, it should say so and offer to connect the visitor with a person. Give medical, legal or financial advice. Clinics, law offices and accountants need especially careful limits. Hide the human option. Every chat should make it easy to call, email or request a callback. Collect more personal data than it needs. Ask only for what you will actually use, and say how it will be handled. The Main Types of Hosting Most hosting falls into a handful of categories. The names vary from provider to provider, but the underlying ideas are consistent. Shared hosting. Your site sits on a server alongside many other websites, sharing its processing power, memory, and storage. It is inexpensive and usually comes with a simple control panel. The trade-off is that a busy or badly behaved neighbor can slow your site down, and you have limited control over the server's setup. Virtual private server (VPS). One physical machine is divided into several isolated virtual servers, and you get one of them with a guaranteed share of resources. How to Choose the Right Foundation for Your Website Before a single page is designed, every website project faces a quiet but important decision: how will this site be built and managed? The answer shapes how fast your site loads, how easily your team can update it, how much it costs to maintain, and how exposed it is to security problems. Most business websites end up on one of two paths, a content management system (CMS) or a static site, with a growing middle ground between them. There is no universally right choice. There is only the right choice for how your business actually works. Here is how to think it through. Two Approaches, Explained Simply A traditional CMS such as WordPress, Drupal, or Joomla stores your content in a database. When someone visits a page, the server pulls content from the database, combines it with a template, and builds the page on the spot. You log in to an admin dashboard to edit text, add images, and publish posts. A static site is made of pre-built HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files. The pages are assembled ahead of time, often by a tool called a static site generator such as Hugo, Eleventy, Jekyll, or Astro, and then uploaded to a server or hosting platform. When a visitor arrives, the server simply hands over a finished file. There is no database lookup and no page building in real time. The middle ground is a headless CMS. Services such as Contentful, Sanity, Strapi, or Decap CMS give editors a friendly interface for writing content, while the public website is generated as fast static pages. In reality, most attacks on websites are automated. Bots scan the internet around the clock looking for outdated software, weak passwords, and misconfigured servers. They do not care how big your company is; they care whether your site has an open door. A compromised website can show spam to your customers, redirect them to scam pages, leak form submissions, or be flagged by browsers as unsafe. The encouraging news is that a handful of consistent habits prevent the large majority of everyday problems. Think of website security not as one big lock, but as several layers, each one making the next attack harder. Layer One: Encrypt Everything With HTTPS HTTPS encrypts the connection between your visitor's browser and your website, so information like contact form entries and login details cannot be read or altered in transit. It relies on an SSL/TLS certificate installed on your server. What to check: Every page on your site loads with https:// , not just the checkout or contact page. Visitors who type http:// are automatically redirected to the secure version. Your certificate renews automatically. Free certificates from Let's Encrypt, offered by many hosts, typically renew every 90 days, and an expired certificate triggers alarming browser warnings. There is no "mixed content," meaning images or scripts still loading over plain HTTP. Modern browsers label non-HTTPS pages as "Not secure," so this layer protects your reputation as much as your data.
